page_title: Build Your Own Fast, Persistent KV Store

sources.entry: Ruby: _Build your own fast, persistent KV store in Ruby_

summary.title: Build Your Own Fast, Persistent KV Store
summary.one_liner: Learn how to design a simple persistent key-value store in Ruby using the Bitcask log-structured format, covering binary record layout, CRC checks, and an append-only DiskStore.
keywords: how to store variable length keys and values
takeaways: Bitcask stores key/value records in an append-only file, with one writer process and file rotation at a size threshold.
A record needs key and value sizes plus type info, CRC and timestamp so variable-length data can be read back correctly.
Storing integers as binary (e.g. 4-byte little-endian via Ruby Array.pack) is more compact than writing them as text.
Use fixed-size headers and CRC validation on reads to detect corrupt data; the DiskStore uses an in-memory lookup table to seek to values.
summary.summary: The post walks through building a Bitcask-style persistent key-value store, starting from the Bitcask paper's goals such as low latency, high write throughput, and crash friendliness. It explains the on-disk record format step by step: a 20-byte header with CRC, timestamp, key and value sizes, and type tags, followed by the key and value bytes. It then covers binary encoding with Ruby's Array.pack directives, a Serializer module for serialize and deserialize with CRC checks, and a DiskStore class with get and put operations backed by a lookup table. The author leaves out loading an existing data file, pointing to the bitcask-rb GitHub repository for the full code and benchmarks.
